name: Content Security Policy and Browser Hardening
intent: Tell the browser which sources a page may load and run code from, and add a few more response headers, so that an injection flaw in your page does not automatically become a working attack.
scenario: A shop page loads 11 things it needs: its own script, a library from a CDN, an analytics script, an inline bootstrap script, a stylesheet, an image, a payment iframe and an API call. Then a search box turns out to echo input unescaped, and an attacker manages to inject 4 more: an inline script, an onerror handler, a script from their own server, and a script that abuses an allowed CDN.
problem: Fixing the injection flaw is the real cure, but there will be another one. Without a policy, the browser runs whatever script appears in the page, wherever it came from. A Content Security Policy (CSP) lets the page say what is allowed, but a policy that is too loose (allow-lists plus unsafe-inline) protects almost nothing, and one that is too strict breaks the page the day it ships.

howItWorks.title: A policy is a list of allowed sources per kind of resource
howItWorks.text: The server sends a Content-Security-Policy header. Each directive covers one kind of load: script-src for scripts, style-src, img-src, frame-src, connect-src for fetch and XHR, and default-src as the fallback for any directive not listed. A source can be 'self', a host, a nonce, a hash, or a keyword. A load that no source allows is blocked and, if you set a reporting endpoint, reported.

howItWorks.title: Why unsafe-inline defeats it
howItWorks.text: Most injected attacks are inline: a script tag or an event handler written into the HTML. A policy that allows 'unsafe-inline' for scripts allows exactly those, so the policy no longer stops the attack it exists for. Host allow-lists also fall short: if an allowed host serves attacker-chosen code (an open callback endpoint, a hosted library with a gadget), the attacker's script runs from a source you listed.

howItWorks.title: Nonces and hashes allow your inline code only
howItWorks.text: With a nonce, the server generates a fresh random value for every response, puts it in the policy and on each of its own script tags; only a script carrying the current nonce runs. A hash lists the digest of a specific inline script instead, which suits static content. An attacker who can inject markup cannot guess a nonce they have not seen. 'strict-dynamic' then extends trust to scripts that a trusted script loads, so you need not list every host. If a nonce is reused or visible in a cached page, it protects nothing.

howItWorks.title: Roll out in report-only mode first
howItWorks.text: The Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header evaluates a policy and reports violations without blocking anything. Run it alongside real traffic, fix what it reports (inline handlers rewritten as event listeners, a forgotten third-party script), then switch to enforcing. Collecting reports also shows you which third parties your pages really load. Keep one policy per page type if they differ.

howItWorks.title: Other headers each close one door
howItWorks.text: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) makes the browser use HTTPS only for your site once it has seen the header. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops the browser from guessing that a file is a script. The frame-ancestors directive controls who may embed your page in a frame, which stops clickjacking. Cookies with SameSite=Lax or Strict, plus HttpOnly and Secure, limit what a stolen or cross-site request can do. None is a replacement for fixing injection, and none replaces another.

pros: Turns many injection flaws from working attacks into blocked requests and reports
Reports show attempted attacks and unexpected third-party code
Nonce or hash policies protect against injected inline script without allow-lists
The other headers are one line each and rarely break anything
cons: A strict policy needs real work: inline handlers and inline styles must go or be tagged
Third-party scripts and tag managers that inject more scripts are hard to fit
Nonces need a fresh value per response, which complicates full-page caching
Browser support and details vary, so test in the browsers you support
whenToUse: Any site that renders user-controlled content or sets login cookies
A nonce-based policy for dynamic pages, hashes for static ones
The simple headers (nosniff, frame-ancestors, HSTS) on every site
whenNotToUse: CSP as a replacement for output encoding and input handling: it is a second layer
A copy-pasted policy that nobody has tested against the real page
'unsafe-inline' for scripts, or a wide allow-list of CDNs, if the aim is to stop injection
pitfalls: Adding 'unsafe-inline' to script-src to make the page work again, which removes the main protection
Allow-listing a large shared CDN that can serve attacker-chosen code
Using the same nonce on every response, or putting it in a page that is cached
Enforcing straight away without a report-only period, and breaking checkout on a Friday
A policy so strict, such as default-src 'none' with nothing added back, that the page is blank
Setting headers only on the HTML page and forgetting error pages, redirects or other hosts
Treating a clean report as proof of safety: reports are blocked attempts, not a scan

roles.label: Browser
roles.description: Enforces the policy on every load.

roles.label: Shop server
roles.description: Sends the page and the policy headers.

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: Can inject markup into the page through a flaw.

quiz.question: A site sets script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://cdn.example. A search box echoes input unescaped, and an attacker injects an inline script tag. What happens?
options: It is blocked, because the page lists only trusted sources and this one is not listed
It runs, because 'unsafe-inline' allows inline scripts, including injected ones
It is blocked, because the CSP header detects content that came from user input
It runs only if the attacker's script is loaded from the cdn.example host by src
quiz.explanation: 'unsafe-inline' allows every inline script, and the browser cannot tell yours from the attacker's. CSP does not detect user content. The host list matters only for scripts loaded by src, so this inline script needs no listed host.

quiz.question: A team wants to deploy a strict CSP on a busy checkout page without breaking it. What is the safest first step?
options: Enforce the policy at night, when traffic is low, and watch the error rate until morning
Start with default-src 'none' and add back whatever breaks as users complain
Add 'unsafe-inline' for scripts so nothing breaks, then tighten it later on
Send it as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, fix the reported violations, then enforce
quiz.explanation: Report-only evaluates the policy against real traffic and blocks nothing, so you find the inline handlers and forgotten third-party scripts before customers do. Starting from nothing allowed breaks the page, and unsafe-inline gives up the protection you wanted.

quiz.question: A page uses a nonce-based CSP, but the nonce is the same string in every response. An attacker finds an injection point. Why does the policy no longer help?
options: The attacker reads the nonce from an earlier response and adds it to the injected script
A nonce is only checked for external scripts and is never checked for inline ones
The nonce is hashed by the browser, so repeating the same value changes the hash
Browsers ignore a nonce whenever the same policy also contains strict-dynamic
quiz.explanation: A nonce works only because the attacker cannot know the value for this response. If it repeats, they have seen it, so an injected script that carries it is allowed. It must be fresh and unpredictable per response. Nonces apply to inline scripts too, and strict-dynamic is designed to work with them.
